comments.content: When the file doesn't exist, this writes `JSON.stringify(updates, null, 2)` directly. If `updates` contains resolved env var values (which it will, since `saveSettings` passes the merged settings that have already been resolved via `resolveEnvVarsInObject`), the newly created file will contain the resolved secret values instead of the `$VAR` references. Consider applying `restoreEnvVarReferences` here too, or at least documenting this behavior.

`applyUpdates` mutates `current` in place and returns it. Since `parsed` is the result of `parse(originalContent)`, this is fine for the current call site, but the function name and signature suggest a pure update. More importantly, when `updates` contains a key whose value is `undefined`, `Object.entries` will include it and `result[key] = undefined` will be set, which `comment-json`'s `stringify` may serialize as `null` or omit inconsistently. Consider skipping `undefined` values explicitly.

`restoreEnvVarReferences` uses `mapping.path.join('.')` as the map key. If any settings key contains a literal `.` character, this will produce collisions (e.g. path `['a.b']` and `['a','b']` both become `'a.b'`). Use a more robust key (e.g. `JSON.stringify(mapping.path)`) to avoid ambiguity.

`restoreEnvVarsRecursive` only recurses into plain objects, not arrays. If an env var reference lives inside an array element (e.g. `mcpServers` entries stored as arrays, or any list-valued setting), the reference will not be restored and the resolved secret will be written to disk. Consider handling arrays by iterating indices.

`trackEnvVarMappings` uses `for (const key in obj)` which iterates inherited enumerable properties. Since `obj`/`originalObj` come from parsed JSON this is usually safe, but for robustness (and to match the prototype-pollution hardening elsewhere in this file) prefer `Object.keys(obj)` or `Object.entries(obj)`.

The env var regex `/^\$(?:(\w+)|{([^}]+)})$/` only matches a value that is *entirely* a single env var reference. Values like `"prefix-$VAR"` or `"${A}-${B}"` won't be tracked, so if such a value is resolved and later saved, the resolved secret will be persisted to disk. Confirm this is intentional; if not, the regex should match embedded references too.

`structuredClone(systemSettings)` etc. are taken *after* `loadEnvironment(tempMergedSettings)` but the originals are captured right before `resolveEnvVarsInObject`. That's correct for tracking, but note that `trackEnvVarMappings` is called with `(resolved, original)` — verify the argument order matches the function signature `(obj, originalObj)`. It does here, but the naming in the call site (`systemSettings, systemOriginal`) is easy to invert in future edits; consider a named-args or clearer naming.

`this.envVarMappings.get(scope) || []` — the map is populated for System/User/Workspace in `loadSettings`, but if a new `SettingScope` is added later (or if `setValue` is called with a scope not in the map), the fallback `[]` silently disables env var restoration and the resolved secret will be written to disk. Consider logging a warning or throwing when the scope is missing from `envVarMappings`.

`updateSettingsFilePreservingFormat` swallows parse errors internally (logs and returns without writing). The previous `fs.writeFileSync` would throw on failure and be caught by the surrounding try/catch, which logs `'Error saving user settings file:'`. Now a corrupted settings file will silently fail to save with a different error message and no indication to the caller that the save did not happen. Consider returning a boolean or rethrowing so callers can react.
